sentences.text: "Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance.
The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just.
What would be "just" compensation is a vexed question.
There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a limb.
Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations.
It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any.
Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non- pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial;
(iii) other material loss.

So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, hardship, discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental stress in life."

sentences.text: The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

[See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR 50 : (1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .]

As per the material on record, respondent no. 1/ Raju, was the driver of the offending vehicle, respondent no. 2/ Deepak, was the registered owner,
and respondent no. 3/ Bittu, was in possession of the vehicle.

Despite being directed,
the respondents failed to furnish any security deposit.

Respondent no. 2, Deepak (the registered owner), in his reply stated that he had sold the vehicle to respondent no. 3,
Bittu, on 16.02.2018, and placed on record a Sale Agreement by way of affidavit along with Form 29 and Form 30 as part of the DAR.
However, no evidence has been led by him to establish due transfer of ownership in accordance with law.

It is a settled legal position that mere execution of sale documents does not discharge the registered owner of liability unless the vehicle stands transferred in the records of the registering authority.
Since no such transfer took place, Deepak continued to be the registered owner on the date of accident and, therefore, remains liable to pay compensation.

Keeping in view the above discussion, it is held that entire liability befalls on R-1/ driver, R-2/ registered owner & R-3/ possession holder and they are held to be liable to pay the compensation and award amount in question to the claimant as held above with simple interest at the rate of 7.5% p.a. from the date of filing of DAR till its actual MACT No. 108/2020 Majnu Vs. 6. Findings:
Whether the injured persons suffered injuries in a road Traffic accident on 01.09.2019 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. DL 1LL 0323 being driven by R-1 and owned by R-2? OPP 6(a).
opennyai_summary.facts:
As per the statement, the injured persons were sleeping / sitting/ moving on the central verge when the speeding, recklessly driven and uncontrolled offending vehicle crashed into the divider and ran over the injured persons.
Central verge /
road divider was no place for movement of the vehicle and therefore, presence of persons on the divider/ footpath / central verge cannot be taken as a contributing factor towards the accident.
Notice u/s 133 MV Act was served upon the registered owner of the damaged offending vehicle seized from the spot of accident who informed about the actual owner/ possession holder who in turn produced the driver of the offending vehicle at the time of accident.
R-1 refused to participate in the TIP proceedings leading to adverse inference against him for causing the accident.
Site plan and mechanical inspection of the offending vehicle form the basis for chargesheeting R-1 for causing death of persons and injuring others due to rash driving of the offending vehicle.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Any evidence has also not been led by R-1.
Respondents have also settled the other connected matters pertaining to same accident and paid the compensation amount.
It is settled that filing of charge sheet itself is a significant step towards the inference of negligence on the part of driver of the offending vehicle.
MACT No. 108/2020 Majnu Vs. Raju & Ors.
It is also settled that adverse inference can be drawn against the driver of the offending vehicle in case he does not appear as a witness to depose and clarify about his stand in respect of the accident.
6(b) It is a well-established legal principle that negligence in motor accident cases should be determined based on the preponderance of probabilities, not on proof beyond reasonable doubt.
The facts and circumstances must be considered in a broad and practical manner.
It is also settled that proceedings under the Motor Vehicles Act are different from regular civil suits and are not strictly governed by the technical rules of the Indian Evidence Act.
(as observed by Their Lordships of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors., (2009) 13 SCC 530 further referred and relied by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in recent pronouncement in the case of Mathew Alexander vs Mohammed Shafi SLP (Crl)
No.8211 of 2022).
Before putting in frame the position of law, it is noted that the process of determining the compensation by the court is essentially a very difficult task and can never be an exact science.
Perfect compensation is hardly possible, more so in claims of injury and disability.
(As observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Sidram Vs. The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Company Ltd, SLP (Civil) No. 19277 of 2019).
[Support drawn from Govind Yadav v. New India Insurance Co. Ltd., (2011) 10 SCC 683] .
. 9 of 18
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
[See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR 50 : (1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .]
What usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability--Item (ii)(a).
13. It is settled proposition of law, as held in catena of judgments that "just compensation" should include all elements that would go to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in, before the occurrence of the accident.
Whilst no amount of money or other material compensation can erase the trauma, pain and suffering that a victim undergoes after a serious accident, (or replace the loss of a loved one), monetary compensation is the manner known to law, whereby society assures some measure of restitution to those who survive, and the victims who have to face their lives.
17(a) It is settled that any fixed rate of interest cannot be prescribed for all cases at all times and would largely depend upon the prevailing rate of interest as per the applicable guidelines.
(Reliance placed upon National Insurance Company Ltd Vs. Yad Ram MAC APP 526/2018 also referred and relied in case of The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd Vs. Sohan Lal & Ors. MAC APP 70/2024 of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court).
18. Liability:-
18(a) In the present case, the offending vehicle was admittedly not insured, which is a matter of record.
It is a settled legal position that mere execution of sale documents does not discharge the registered owner of liability unless the vehicle stands transferred in the records of the registering authority.
Since no such transfer took place, Deepak continued to be the registered owner on the date of accident and, therefore, remains liable to pay compensation.
